successor: Saba under highland-tribe kings at Marib (rival Himyarite kingdom kept Zafar)
source1: Jérémie Schiettecatte, 'Sabaʾ', Thematic Dictionary of Ancient Arabia, online ed. 2024 (doi 10.60667/tdaa-0191) - https://ancientarabia.huma-num.fr/dictionary/definition/saba
source2: Iwona Gajda, 'Ḥimyar', Thematic Dictionary of Ancient Arabia, online ed. 2023 - https://ancientarabia.huma-num.fr/dictionary/definition/himyar
notes: Himyar-Saba union ('kings of Saba and dhu-Raydan') split: Marib passed to Sabaean highland-tribe kings, Himyar kept Zafar; both claimed the title. Split dated end-1st c. (Gajda) or c.150-160 (Schiettecatte). No capital listed; T5/S3 arguable depending on core.

successor: Kingdom of Prussia (Warsaw, after Russian occupation 1794-96), with Russia and Austria
source2: Library of Congress Federal Research Division, Poland: A Country Study (ed. G. E. Curtis, 1992), 'The Three Partitions, 1764-95' - http://countrystudies.us/poland/11.htm
notes: Database end 1791 (May Constitution) too early. Russian and Prussian armies crushed the 1794 Kosciuszko rising (Suvorov's forces prevailed); Third Partition 1795 dissolved the state, Warsaw to Prussia. Prior crises: Bar and Targowica confederations, 1792 war.

successor: Maukharis and Later Guptas (former Gupta feudatories) in Magadha
source2: A. D. H. Bivar, 'Hephthalites', Encyclopaedia Iranica (2003) - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hephthalites ; also Britannica 'Mihirakula' - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mihirakula
notes: Huna (Alkhan) invasions hit the west but were repelled by Guptas and Yasodharman; Magadha not conquered. Empire dwindled as feudatories (Maukharis, Later Guptas) became independent; Maukharis gained some control of Magadha. Last main-line king c.540-550.

Chola Parantaka I (r. 907-c.955), 'destroyer of Madurai', defeated Pandya Rajasimha and Sri Lankan allies (Vellur, c.915), annexing the Pandya country; the king fled to Lanka. Second source could not be opened (fetch rate-limited).

successor: Kahuripan Kingdom (Airlangga, from 1019) after sack by Haji Wurawari of Lwaram
notes: Pucangan inscription: vassal Haji Wurawari of Lwaram sacked capital Wwatan c.1016 (older reading 1006), killing Dharmawangsa; Airlangga refounded the kingdom 1019. Srivijayan instigation hypothesised (would make T2). No scholarly page could be opened (rate limits).

successor: Hyksos 15th Dynasty (Avaris) in the Memphite/Itjtawy region; Theban dynasties in Upper Egypt
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'ancient Egypt: The Second Intermediate Period' (13th dynasty c.1759-c.1630 BCE; 15th dynasty c.1630-c.1530 BCE) - https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Egypt/The-Second-Intermediate-Period
notes: Core = Itjtawy (capital at 1700 BCE). 13th Dynasty lasted to c.1650-1630 BCE (database end too early); Memphite region then under Hyksos. Ryholt: Hyksos conquest; Ben Tor: prior abandonment for Thebes. 14th Dynasty breakaway preceded.

source2: Mohammad Javad Sheikh-ol-Islami, 'Aḥmad Shah Qājār', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/ahmad-shah-qajar
notes: Majles deposed Ahmad Shah and ended Qajar rule (31 Oct 1925), entrusting government to PM Reza Khan; Constituent Assembly crowned him. Constitution, Majles and ministries continued. Prior crises: Constitutional Revolution, 1909 deposition, WWI occupation, 1921 coup.

source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Xin dynasty' - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Xin-dynasty (same publisher; no independent source could be opened)
notes: Regent Wang Mang, a consort-clan insider, became acting emperor (6 CE) and took the throne (9 CE) within the Chang'an court and bureaucracy; Liu line interrupted. Revolts of Liu Chong (6) and Zhai Yi (7 CE) preceded. T1c arguable.

successor: Zunghar Khanate (Galdan), then Qing after Dolon Nor 1691 and Jao Modo 1696
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mongolia: The ascendancy of the Manchu' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Mongolia/The-ascendancy-of-the-Manchu
notes: Galdan's Zunghars invaded Khalkha 1688, fighting at Erdene Zuu (Karakorum) and driving the khans into Inner Mongolia; they submitted to Qing at Dolon Nor 1691. Northern Yuan great khanate already ended 1634-35. Tusheet-Zasagt war preceded.

Torodbe Muslim clerics of Futa itself, led by Sulayman Bal (from c.1769) then Abdul Kader Kane, overthrew the Denianke satigis and set up an elective almamate in 1776. Prior crises: Moorish raids and tribute, Denianke succession wars.
